summary: AI observability has become essential in 2026 as non-deterministic LLM failures cannot be reproduced with traditional logs, making span-based trace replay and LLM-specific evaluation baseline requirements. Despite market maturity, 63.4% of enterprises still cite inadequate observability tooling as a major barrier, while adoption grows rapidly (New Relic reports 30% QoQ growth in AI monitoring). Choosing the right tool depends on licensing, deployment model, evaluation needs, and whether you prioritize cost tracking or deep debugging.

tools.name: LangSmith
tools.monitors: End-to-end LLM application traces, token usage, latency, costs, and evaluation metrics, with deep native support for LangChain and LangGraph workflows.
features: Detailed trace and span visualization for agent workflows
Cost analytics per run and per project
tools.pricing: ~£80/month; seat-based plus usage pricing. Free developer tier available; most expensive of the compared tools. Setup ~30 mins.
tools.best_for: Teams already building on LangChain/LangGraph who want zero-config auto-instrumentation and comprehensive tracing/evaluation.

tools.name: Helicone
tools.monitors: API request/response logs, per-user and per-department cost tracking, token usage, latency, and budget consumption via a lightweight proxy.
features: Excellent cost analytics with per-user cost tracking
Budget alerts and spend governance in under 5 minutes
tools.pricing: ~£20/month; request/usage-based model with a generous free tier. Setup ~2 mins, no maintenance.
tools.best_for: Teams that want the simplest setup and the best cost visibility across users/departments without architectural overhead.

tools.name: Weights & Biases (W&B Weave)
tools.monitors: Unified ML experiment tracking and LLM application traces, including model performance, token usage, evaluations, and dataset versioning across both ML and LLM workloads.
features: W&B Weave for LLM trace logging and visualization
Unified monitoring across ML training and LLM inference
Experiment tracking and model registry integration
tools.pricing: Free personal tier; team/enterprise plans are seat- and usage-based (custom enterprise pricing).
tools.best_for: Teams running both traditional ML and LLM workloads who need a single platform for experiments plus LLM observability.

tools.name: Arize AI (Phoenix)
tools.monitors: LLM and ML model performance in production, including drift, embeddings, hallucination/quality metrics, traces, and token/cost usage; Phoenix offers open-source OpenTelemetry-based tracing.
tools.pricing: Phoenix is free and open-source; Arize cloud platform uses usage-based pricing with free and enterprise tiers.
tools.best_for: ML/LLM teams needing production-grade drift detection, embedding analysis, and open, framework-agnostic tracing.

tools.name: LangFuse
tools.monitors: LLM application traces, token usage, costs, latency, prompt performance, and evaluation scores, with both cloud and self-hosted deployment options.
tools.pricing: Cloud free tier for <50K events, then ~£20/month for 500K; self-hosted is ~£30/month infra cost (free software) plus ~2hrs/month maintenance. Setup ~30 mins.
tools.best_for: Cost-conscious teams wanting open-source flexibility, self-hosting options, and comprehensive (though manual) instrumentation.

tools.name: OpenLLMetry
tools.monitors: LLM calls, traces, token usage, and latency via OpenTelemetry standards, exportable to any OTel-compatible backend across multi-framework stacks.
features: Vendor-neutral, exports to any OTel backend
Automatic instrumentation of popular LLM SDKs
Works across any framework or stack
tools.pricing: Free and open-source (SDK); costs depend on the chosen OTel backend/destination.
tools.best_for: Multi-framework teams that want vendor-neutral, standards-based tracing integrated into an existing observability stack.

cost_tips: Implement per-user and per-department cost tracking with budget alerts (e.g., via Helicone) to catch runaway spend early and attribute costs accurately.
Cache repeated or similar requests and use prompt/response caching to avoid paying for duplicate LLM calls.
Right-size your models by routing simpler tasks to smaller/cheaper models and reserving flagship models for complex reasoning, and trim prompt/context length to reduce token consumption.

Consolidate observability into tools you already subscribe to rather than adding new vendors, and use trace-level replay to debug non-deterministic failures efficiently instead of re-running expensive calls.
